## Before surgery, chemotherapy is a high-stakes test

::: {.motivation-grid}
::: {.story-card}
<div class="card-kicker">THE TREATMENT</div>
<div class="card-icon">Before surgery</div>
<p>Chemotherapy can shrink a tumor and reveal how it responds.</p>
:::

::: {.story-card .feature-card}
<div class="card-kicker">THE OUTCOME</div>
<div class="big-stat">≈ 1 in 3</div>
<p>scans came from patients with no remaining invasive cancer at surgery.</p>
:::

::: {.story-card}
<div class="card-kicker">THE QUESTION</div>
<div class="card-icon">Can MRI help?</div>
<p>Could an existing scan give us an earlier clue about treatment response?</p>
:::
:::

<div class="plain-callout">The long-term goal is better evidence for tailoring treatment—not replacing clinical judgment.</div>

::: {.notes}
Many patients with breast cancer receive chemotherapy before surgery. A pathologic
complete response means no invasive cancer remains at surgery; in our dataset,
about one third of scans came from complete responders. Chemotherapy is demanding,
so the motivation is simple: can information already present in an MRI give us an
earlier clue? This is research toward decision support, not a clinical tool or a
replacement for physicians.
:::

## An MRI “movie” shows more than anatomy

<div class="lead-line">After contrast is injected, repeated MRI frames reveal <strong>how it appears through the breast’s vessels over time.</strong></div>

![](figures/pipeline.svg){.nostretch width="94%" fig-align="center"}

::: {.three-facts}
<div><strong>179</strong><span>analyzed exams</span></div>
<div><strong>143</strong><span>patients</span></div>
<div><strong>13–24</strong><span>frames per MRI movie</span></div>
:::

::: {.notes}
These scans are closer to a short movie than a still picture. A contrast agent
enters the blood, and the scanner repeatedly records where it appears. We isolate
the vessels, reduce them to centerlines, and turn the branching structure into data
a model can read. The study included 179 exams from 143 patients, with 13 to 24
frames per movie. That gives us both vessel shape and change over time.
:::

## We asked whether the vessel **map** adds value

::: {.map-question}
::: {.network-panel aria-label="A branching vessel graph with connected nodes"}
<svg viewBox="0 0 500 300" role="img" aria-label="Connected branching vessel map">
  <g class="edges">
    <line x1="70" y1="150" x2="170" y2="150"/>
    <line x1="170" y1="150" x2="270" y2="75"/>
    <line x1="170" y1="150" x2="280" y2="155"/>
    <line x1="170" y1="150" x2="255" y2="235"/>
    <line x1="280" y1="155" x2="395" y2="120"/>
    <line x1="280" y1="155" x2="395" y2="205"/>
  </g>
  <g class="nodes">
    <circle cx="70" cy="150" r="17"/><circle cx="170" cy="150" r="21"/>
    <circle cx="270" cy="75" r="15"/><circle cx="280" cy="155" r="19"/>
    <circle cx="255" cy="235" r="14"/><circle cx="395" cy="120" r="14"/>
    <circle cx="395" cy="205" r="16"/>
  </g>
</svg>
<div class="network-caption"><strong>Graph neural network</strong><br>Each vessel location shares information with its neighbors.</div>
:::

::: {.versus}
<span>VS.</span>
:::

::: {.summary-panel}
<div class="summary-stack">
  <span>How bright?</span>
  <span>How fast?</span>
  <span>How long?</span>
</div>
<div class="network-caption"><strong>Simple summary</strong><br>Average the same vessel measurements across the whole scan.</div>
:::
:::

<div class="question-banner">Does knowing <strong>which vessel connects to which</strong> improve the prediction?</div>

::: {.notes}
My work focused on a graph neural network, or GNN. Think of the vessels as a road
map: each dot is a vessel location, each line is a connection, and neighboring dots
share information. That should help if network patterns matter. But we needed a fair
comparison, so we tested the GNN against a simple model that averages the same
brightness and timing measurements across the scan. The decisive question was
whether the map itself added value.
:::

## Vessel behavior carried a modest signal

<div class="score-explainer">Ranking score: <strong>50 = chance</strong> · <strong>100 = perfect</strong></div>

::: {.score-chart}
<div class="score-axis"><span>50</span><span>60</span><span>70</span></div>

<div class="score-row">
  <div class="score-label">Simple vessel averages</div>
  <div class="score-track"><div class="score-bar simple" style="width:57%"></div></div>
  <div class="score-value">61.4</div>
</div>

<div class="score-row">
  <div class="score-label">Graph neural network</div>
  <div class="score-track"><div class="score-bar gnn" style="width:58%"></div></div>
  <div class="score-value">61.6</div>
</div>
:::

::: {.result-grid}
::: {.result-card .positive}
<strong>Something is there.</strong>

Vessel enhancement ranked responders above non-responders about 61 times out of 100.
:::

::: {.result-card .caution}
<strong>But the estimate is uncertain.</strong>

Differences in scan timing may explain part of it; the defensible range is roughly **54–61**.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
The vessel measurements contained a modest signal. This ranking score uses 50 for
chance and 100 for perfect. Both models scored about 61: given one responder and one
non-responder, the model ranks the responder higher about 61 times out of 100. That
is better than chance, but far from clinical readiness. Scan timing also differed
across the dataset, and several measurements depend on timing. After auditing that
issue, the defensible range is roughly 54 to 61—not one precise headline number.
:::

## The clearest result came from deleting the graph

::: {.ablation-wrap}
::: {.ablation-panel}
<div class="mini-title">Real vessel connections</div>
<svg viewBox="0 0 360 220" role="img" aria-label="Nodes joined by vessel connections">
  <g class="edges">
    <line x1="45" y1="110" x2="130" y2="110"/><line x1="130" y1="110" x2="210" y2="55"/>
    <line x1="130" y1="110" x2="220" y2="120"/><line x1="130" y1="110" x2="205" y2="180"/>
    <line x1="220" y1="120" x2="315" y2="95"/><line x1="220" y1="120" x2="310" y2="170"/>
  </g>
  <g class="nodes">
    <circle cx="45" cy="110" r="14"/><circle cx="130" cy="110" r="18"/>
    <circle cx="210" cy="55" r="13"/><circle cx="220" cy="120" r="16"/>
    <circle cx="205" cy="180" r="12"/><circle cx="315" cy="95" r="12"/>
    <circle cx="310" cy="170" r="13"/>
  </g>
</svg>
<div class="ablation-score">61.6</div>
:::

<div class="delete-arrow"><span>remove every<br>connection</span><strong>→</strong></div>

::: {.ablation-panel .dropped}
<div class="mini-title">Measurements only</div>
<svg viewBox="0 0 360 220" role="img" aria-label="The same nodes with all connections removed">
  <g class="nodes">
    <circle cx="45" cy="110" r="14"/><circle cx="130" cy="110" r="18"/>
    <circle cx="210" cy="55" r="13"/><circle cx="220" cy="120" r="16"/>
    <circle cx="205" cy="180" r="12"/><circle cx="315" cy="95" r="12"/>
    <circle cx="310" cy="170" r="13"/>
  </g>
</svg>
<div class="ablation-score">61.8</div>
:::
:::

<div class="takeaway-banner"><strong>Prediction did not get worse.</strong> The current GNN mostly used vessel measurements—not their connections.</div>

::: {.notes}
The most informative experiment was simple: we deleted every graph connection. If
the model used the vessel map, performance should fall. It did not. The disconnected
model scored 61.8, essentially the same as 61.6 with the real network. Other ways of
drawing the graph also produced no reliable improvement. This does not prove vessel
topology is useless. It tells us something narrower: this GNN was mostly ignoring
the network structure.
:::

## A negative result saved us from the wrong next step

::: {.lesson-grid}
::: {.lesson-card}
<div class="lesson-number">1</div>
<strong>Keep the useful signal</strong>
<p>How vessels enhance over time is worth studying.</p>
:::

::: {.lesson-card}
<div class="lesson-number">2</div>
<strong>Stop adding static complexity</strong>
<p>More graph types and more static layers were not answering the real question.</p>
:::

::: {.lesson-card}
<div class="lesson-number">3</div>
<strong>Learn the movie itself</strong>
<p>The next model should learn contrast flow through time before predicting response.</p>
:::
:::

<div class="plain-callout">A “no improvement” result is valuable when it tells us what to stop—and what to test next.</div>

::: {.notes}
This negative result changed the project’s direction. We keep the finding that
enhancement behavior carries some signal, stop spending time on more static graph
variations, and return to what makes this dataset special: it is a movie. The first
model compressed each vessel curve into a few measurements before learning, which
may discard the pattern we care about. A good negative result removes an
unproductive branch and sharpens the next experiment.
:::

## Next: learn contrast flow before treatment response

<div class="planned-badge">PLANNED NEXT EXPERIMENT — NOT YET A RESULT</div>

::: {.movie-strip}
<div class="movie-frame"><span>1</span><i class="pulse p1"></i></div>

<div class="movie-frame"><span>3</span><i class="pulse p3"></i></div>
<div class="movie-arrow">predict →</div>
<div class="movie-frame future"><span>4</span><strong>?</strong></div>
<div class="movie-frame future"><span>5</span><strong>?</strong></div>
:::

::: {.next-grid}
<div><strong>~1,000 exams</strong><span>Learn without treatment labels</span></div>
<div><strong>With vs. without the map</strong><span>Test whether connections help</span></div>
<div><strong>Before vs. after pretraining</strong><span>Test whether learning the movie improves response prediction</span></div>
:::

::: {.notes}
The next experiment is self-supervised pretraining: show the model three MRI frames
and ask it to predict the next two. We can use roughly one thousand exams without
treatment labels, forcing the model to learn change through time. Then we compare
the same temporal model with and without vessel connections, each started from
scratch or from pretraining. This separates two questions: does learning the movie
help, and does the vessel map add anything beyond each location’s own curve?
:::

## What should you remember?

::: {.remember-grid}
::: {.remember-card}
<span>1</span>
<p><strong>Vessel contrast behavior</strong> carries modest—but uncertain—information about response.</p>
:::

::: {.remember-card}
<span>2</span>
<p>Our first <strong>graph neural network did not benefit</strong> from the vessel connections.</p>
:::

::: {.remember-card}
<span>3</span>
<p>That result redirected us toward <strong>learning contrast flow through time</strong>.</p>
:::
:::

<div class="closing-line">A simpler model won this round—and showed us exactly what to test next.</div>

::: {.notes}
Vessel enhancement behavior contains modest, uncertain information about response.
Our first GNN did not gain from the connections in the vessel map. That negative
result gave us a better next test: learn change through time, then ask whether the
graph finally adds value. A simpler model won this round—and showed us exactly where
the current approach falls short.
:::
